answers.question: q_python
answers.label: good
answers.text: The default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, not every time it is called. So if the default is an empty list and the function appends to it, every call that uses the default shares the same list, and items from earlier calls leak into later ones. The fix is to use None as the default and create a new list inside the function, like if items is None then items equals an empty list. I hit this once in my internship in a helper that collected log lines, and the logs kept growing between requests until I changed the default to None.

answers.question: q_python
answers.label: medium
answers.text: I think it is bad practice because the list can keep old values between calls. You should use None instead and then make the list inside the function. I am not completely sure why it happens though.

answers.question: q_python
answers.label: bad
answers.text: Um, mutable means it can change, so maybe it is slower? I usually just use lists everywhere and it works fine.

answers.question: q_sql
answers.label: good
answers.text: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens, and HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and the aggregates are computed. So if I want customers with more than five orders in 2025, I put the date condition in WHERE, group by customer id, and then use HAVING count of orders greater than five. You cannot use an aggregate like COUNT in WHERE because the groups do not exist yet at that point. Filtering early in WHERE is also cheaper because fewer rows reach the grouping step.

answers.question: q_sql
answers.label: medium
answers.text: WHERE is used to filter rows and HAVING is used with GROUP BY. So HAVING is for groups, like when you use COUNT. I mostly use WHERE in my queries.

answers.question: q_sql
answers.label: bad
answers.text: They are basically the same thing, HAVING is just the newer way to write WHERE. You can use either one.

answers.question: q_ml
answers.label: good
answers.text: Overfitting is when a model learns the noise in the training data instead of the general pattern, so training accuracy is high but validation accuracy is much lower. I detect it by comparing training and validation curves. To prevent it you can get more data, use a simpler model, add regularization like L2 or dropout, use cross-validation, and stop early when the validation loss starts rising. In my crop disease project the CNN hit 99 percent on training but 80 on validation, so I added data augmentation and early stopping, and the test accuracy went up to 91 percent.

answers.question: q_ml
answers.label: medium
answers.text: Overfitting is when the model is too good on the training data and not good on test data. You can prevent it with regularization or by getting more data. I used a validation set in my project.

answers.question: q_ml
answers.label: bad
answers.text: Overfitting is when you train the model for too long and the computer overheats, so you should train on a smaller laptop or use the cloud.

answers.question: q_rag
answers.label: good
answers.text: RAG means you retrieve relevant documents first and give them to the language model as context, so it answers from your data instead of only its training data. To build one, I split documents into chunks, embed each chunk, and store the vectors in an index. At query time I embed the question, retrieve the top chunks, and put them in the prompt with an instruction to answer only from the context and cite sources. In my campus policy assistant I used LangChain with FAISS over 300 PDFs, and I evaluated faithfulness on 50 questions. The main trade-offs are chunk size, retrieval quality, and the risk the model ignores the context, so I would also add hybrid keyword search and an evaluation set.

answers.question: q_rag
answers.label: medium
answers.text: RAG is retrieval augmented generation. You search your documents and then give the results to the LLM so it can answer better. You use embeddings and a vector database for the search part. I built a chatbot like this for university policies.

answers.question: q_rag
answers.label: bad
answers.text: RAG is when you train a new model from scratch on your documents. It is like fine tuning but bigger. I have not really used it.

answers.question: q_api
answers.label: good
answers.text: I use 200 for a successful read, 201 when something is created, and 204 when there is nothing to return, like after a delete. For client errors, 400 is a malformed request, 422 is valid JSON that fails validation, which FastAPI returns automatically, 401 means not authenticated and 403 means authenticated but not allowed, 404 is not found, and 429 is for rate limiting with a Retry-After header. 500 is an unexpected server error, and 503 means a dependency is down. Using the right codes lets clients decide whether to retry, for example retrying a 503 but never a 400.

answers.question: q_api
answers.label: medium
answers.text: 200 means OK, 404 means not found, and 500 is a server error. I think 401 is for when you are not logged in. In my FastAPI project I mostly returned 200.

answers.question: q_api
answers.label: bad
answers.text: I just return 200 for everything and put an error message in the body. Status codes are not that important if the frontend reads the message.

answers.question: q_git
answers.label: good
answers.text: First I pull the latest main into my branch, then Git marks the conflicting files. I open each one, look at both sides between the conflict markers, and decide what the combined code should be, which sometimes means asking the teammate who wrote the other change. Then I remove the markers, run the tests to make sure nothing broke, stage the files and commit the merge. To avoid big conflicts I keep branches short-lived and pull from main often. During my internship I resolved a conflict in a shared config file this way after checking with the other developer.

answers.question: q_git
answers.label: medium
answers.text: Git shows you the conflict in the file with arrows and equal signs. You pick which version you want, delete the markers, and then commit again. Sometimes I use the VS Code buttons for that.

answers.question: q_git
answers.label: bad
answers.text: I usually delete my local folder and clone the repository again, then copy my changes back in.

answers.question: q_docker
answers.label: good
answers.text: Docker packages an application with its dependencies into an image, and a container is a running instance of that image. That means the app runs the same on my laptop, in CI and on the server, which removes the it works on my machine problem. Containers are lighter than virtual machines because they share the host kernel. I write a Dockerfile starting from a slim Python base image, copy requirements first so the dependency layer is cached, then copy the code. For the FastAPI service in my project I used a container so my teammate could run it with one command, and I kept secrets out of the image by passing them as environment variables.

answers.question: q_docker
answers.label: medium
answers.text: Docker lets you put your app in a container so it runs the same everywhere. It is like a lightweight virtual machine. I have used it to run a database locally.

answers.question: q_docker
answers.label: bad
answers.text: Docker is a cloud company like AWS where you host websites. I have not used it.

answers.question: q_team
answers.label: good
answers.text: In my final-year project, two of us disagreed about whether to use a vector database service or a local FAISS index, and it was blocking our sprint. My task was to get us to a decision within the week. I suggested we list the requirements, cost, offline use and setup time, and each of us built a one-day prototype. I measured retrieval latency for both and shared a short comparison in our group chat. The data showed FAISS was fast enough and free, so we chose it, and my teammate took ownership of the indexing code. We delivered on time, and I learned that a small experiment ends a debate faster than arguing opinions.

answers.question: q_team
answers.label: medium
answers.text: In a university project my teammate wanted to use React and I wanted to use plain HTML. We talked about it and in the end we used React because more people knew it. It worked out fine.

answers.question: q_team

answers.question: q_fail
answers.label: good
answers.text: During my internship I was asked to clean a customer dataset before a churn model was trained. I was in a hurry and dropped every row with a missing value without checking, which removed almost a third of the data and mostly the newer customers. When my supervisor saw the model's odd results, I traced it back to my cleaning step and told her directly that it was my mistake. I re-ran the cleaning with imputation for the numeric columns and documented every step in the notebook, and the model's validation score went back to normal. Since then I always check how many rows each cleaning step removes and write that down.

answers.question: q_explain
answers.label: good
answers.text: My project is like a helpful librarian for university rules. Students usually have to dig through hundreds of pages to find out, say, how to apply for a scholarship. With my assistant, you just type the question in normal words, it finds the few paragraphs that talk about it, and it writes a short answer and shows you which document it came from so you can check. I tested it with 50 real student questions, and it made up answers far less often than a normal chatbot, about 40 percent fewer mistakes. It saves students time and stops wrong information spreading.

answers.question: q_explain
answers.label: medium
answers.text: It is a chatbot that answers questions about university policies. It uses AI to search the documents and then gives you an answer. It uses LangChain and FAISS and FastAPI.

answers.question: q_explain
answers.label: bad
answers.text: It is a RAG pipeline with embeddings in a FAISS vector index, chunked with a recursive splitter at 512 tokens with 50 overlap, and LangChain LCEL chains served by FastAPI with SSE streaming.
